data.title: ADR-005: Synchronous I/O and a mandatory snapshot
body: # ADR-005: Synchronous I/O and a mandatory snapshot
- **Status:** accepted
- **Scope:** architecture
## Context
ADR-002 removed YAML as the main cause of slow reading. What remained was to find out whether that is enough to fit into 200 ms without a snapshot cache.
Measured on 10 000 events in JSON format, scattered across 12 monthly directories (best of 3):
| Way of reading | Time |
| Synchronously (`readFileSync` in a loop) | **140 ms** |
| Asynchronously, concurrency 256 (`Promise.all`) | **182 ms** |
| One compacted file | **6 ms** |
Two things are worth attention.

**Asynchronous reading turned out to be slower than synchronous.** This is counter-intuitive, but the explanation is simple: the files are small and already in the page cache, so the overhead of the promises exceeds the gain from concurrency. Making the core asynchronous "because that is the proper way" would have meant paying 42 ms for a degradation.

**JSON on its own does not save us.** 140 ms of reading + 40 ms of Node startup = 180 ms out of the available 200. The guardrail is formally met, but the margin is 10%, and it disappears on the first repository larger than the test one.
A compacted file gives 6 ms — 23 times faster, and 1.7 MB against 39 MB on disk.
## Alternatives considered
| Option | Pros | Cons |
| Read the journal every time, without a cache | There is no derived state — nothing can fall out of sync | 180 ms out of 200; there is no margin |
| A snapshot cache `state.json` | 6 ms; a margin of 30× | Derived state that can lag behind the journal — reliable invalidation is needed |
| An asynchronous core | "Modern"; does not block the event loop | 42 ms slower; the CLI does nothing in parallel anyway |
## Decision
**The core is synchronous.** The CLI is a process that does one thing and exits; there is nothing in it to block.

**`state.json` is mandatory**, in `.gitignore`. Invalidation is by the ULID of the last event: the snapshot stores the ID of the most recent event it accounted for, and if the journal holds a newer ID, the cache is rebuilt. This is exactly where the choice of ULID from ADR-003 pays off — the comparison "newer/older" is an ordinary string comparison and does not depend on clocks.
The rule that must not be broken: **`state.json` is never a source of truth.** Deleting the file must be safe always. A test for this is a mandatory part of the M4 suite.
## Consequences
- Positive: 6 ms instead of 180; a budget margin for real repositories; synchronous code is noticeably simpler to read and to test.

- Cost of the decision: derived state that can diverge from the journal — a whole source of a class of bugs that would not exist without the cache. Every bug of the "it shows the wrong thing" kind will start with a check exactly here.

- What will have to be reconsidered: if repositories reach hundreds of thousands of events, rebuilding the cache will itself become slow — then incremental access is needed (reading only the events newer than the snapshot), not a full fold of the journal.
